Name: counterfactual_belief_binding
Title: Bound but Not Believed: Testing Whether LLMs Bind Beliefs to the Right Item Under Referential Ambiguity
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's internal belief representation about a specific item is stored via a binding between an item token and a truth-value direction. We hypothesize that belief-vs-fact failures partly arise from *binding errors*: when multiple similar items are in context, the model correctly encodes a truth-value but binds it to the wrong item, and these mis-bindings are (a) diagnosable via a probe that reads out item-conditioned belief, (b) predictive of behavioral belief errors, and (c) causally correctable by re-routing the binding without changing the truth-value representation.
Related Work: Suzgun et al. (Belief in the Machine / KaBLE) show behavioral belief-knowledge-fact confusion. Yang & Jia (2025, retraction) and the referenced belief-vs-knowledge paper use linear belief probes tied to answer correctness. Layer of Truth (Churina et al. 2025) and GeoDe (2026) study truth hyperplanes/belief geometry. Binding-ID work (Feng & Steinhardt 2023) studies entity-attribute binding but not for *belief/truth-value* attribution, and not as an explanation of belief-vs-fact errors. NONE frame belief errors as a *binding* problem between item identity and truth-value under referential ambiguity, nor test causal re-binding as a fix. This recasts belief errors from a truth-direction quality problem into an item-truth binding problem, which is new.
Abstract: Prior work shows LLMs cannot reliably distinguish belief from knowledge and fact, and reads out an internal belief via linear probes on truth directions. But 'belief about a specific item' presupposes the model has correctly bound a truth-value to the intended item. We hypothesize that many belief-vs-fact failures are actually binding errors: the model computes a plausible truth-value but attaches it to the wrong item when several similar items co-occur in context. We test this by constructing multi-item contexts (2-4 similar entities, each paired with a claim of known/unknown/false status) and querying the model's belief about a targeted item. We train item-conditioned belief probes and measure whether the recovered truth-value tracks the queried item or leaks from distractor items. We show that (1) belief representations are item-conditioned and linearly decodable, (2) probe-detected mis-bindings predict behavioral belief errors better than truth-direction quality alone, and (3) causal activation patching of the item-binding subspace (from a single-item control) corrects belief answers without altering the encoded truth-values, whereas patching the truth subspace does the opposite. We introduce a binding-error rate metric and show it grows with item similarity and context length, and that a lightweight attention-based re-binding intervention reduces belief errors while preserving factual QA. This reframes belief-vs-fact confusion as an item-truth binding problem and provides an interpretable, cheap fix. All experiments run on <=9B open-weight models.
Experiments: 1) Dataset: Build multi-item belief scenarios. Each context introduces N=1..4 similar entities (e.g., 'Alice put the ball in the red box; Bob claims the ball is in the blue box; ...'), each associated with a proposition of known-true / known-false / neutral status. Queries target one entity: 'What is the status of X's claim?' / 'Is X's belief correct?'. Include a single-item control (N=1) as the clean binding baseline. ~2-3k items with entity/order/position randomization and an item-similarity axis (very similar vs distinct entity names/attributes). 2) Item-conditioned probing: On Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B (plus base vs chat), extract residual-stream activations at query positions. Train linear probes to predict (a) the truth-value the model assigns and (b) which item the truth-value is bound to. Measure how much the decoded truth-value matches the queried item vs. distractors (binding leakage). 3) Behavioral link: Define binding-error rate = fraction of items where the model's stated belief matches a distractor's status rather than the target's. Test whether probe-detected mis-binding predicts behavioral errors (AUC), and compare against a baseline predictor using only truth-direction confidence. Analyze how binding-error rate scales with N, similarity, and context length. 4) Causal disambiguation: (a) Truth-patch vs binding-patch: patch the truth-value subspace vs. the item-binding subspace (recovered via difference-of-means between clean single-item and ambiguous multi-item states) from a control example; measure which flips the belief answer, testing the double dissociation. (b) Attention re-binding: identify heads whose attention from the query token to item tokens correlates with correct binding; apply a light attention-sharpening/re-routing intervention toward the target item. Measure belief-error reduction and specificity (factual QA retention: MMLU/TriviaQA subset). Metrics: probe accuracy, binding-leakage, binding-error rate, prediction AUC, patch flip-rate and specificity, retained factual accuracy.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Belief and binding subspaces may not cleanly separate with linear probes; we try MLP probes and report negatives as informative. 2) Templated multi-item contexts may induce positional shortcuts; mitigated by randomization and control conditions. 3) The single-item control may not perfectly isolate binding from other confounds; we use multiple control constructions. 4) Attention re-binding may have off-target effects; specificity/retention metrics quantify this. 5) Effects may differ across model families and scale; we report per-condition results rather than universal claims. 6) 'Binding' may only partially explain belief errors; we quantify its contribution rather than claim exclusivity.
